persona.name: Vijaya Deshmukh
persona.background: She runs a small retail shop and often stands for long hours. Over the last few years she has reduced physical activity because exertion brings on symptoms.

diagnoses.name: Chronic stable angina pectoris
diagnoses.description: Paroxysmal, recurrent substernal/precordial constricting discomfort due to transient myocardial ischemia; brought on by exertion/emotion and relieved by rest or sublingual glyceryl trinitrate.

diagnoses.name: Acute coronary syndrome (myocardial infarction/unstable angina)
diagnoses.description: Severe chest discomfort often radiating to left shoulder/neck/arm, typically lasting >20 minutes and may not respond to sublingual GTN; may be associated with breathlessness, nausea/vomiting, collapse/syncope.

diagnoses.name: Acute pericarditis
diagnoses.description: Sharp, constant or pleuritic substernal pain that may be relieved by sitting up and leaning forward; ECG classically shows diffuse ST elevation with PR depression.

diagnoses.name: Myocarditis (acute myocarditis)
diagnoses.description: May present with heart failure, acute myocardial infarction-like picture, or sudden cardiac death; ECG changes common but nonspecific; troponin/CK may be raised early; echo may show LV dysfunction and global hypokinesia.

diagnoses.name: Aortic stenosis
diagnoses.description: Severe AS produces exertional symptoms such as angina/syncope/dyspnea; exam may show parvus et tardus pulse, apicocarotid delay, heaving LV apex, and a harsh diamond-shaped ejection systolic murmur radiating to the carotids with late peaking in severe AS.

diagnoses.name: Aortic regurgitation (chronic)
diagnoses.description: Chronic AR has high-volume collapsing (water-hammer) pulse with wide pulse pressure and peripheral signs; LV impulse laterally displaced; long high-pitched regurgitant murmur.

diagnoses.name: Pulmonary embolism
diagnoses.description: Can present with heaviness/tightness chest pain (whole chest if massive or focal if segmental) with dyspnea and unstable vital signs if massive.

diagnoses.name: Pulmonary arterial hypertension
diagnoses.description: Insidious onset with exertional dyspnea, fatigue, palpitations and near-syncope/syncope; exam may show loud P2, narrow splitting, pulmonary ejection sound, and tricuspid pansystolic murmur if TR present.

diagnoses.name: Constrictive pericarditis
diagnoses.description: Causes venous congestion with elevated JVP, often Kussmaul’s sign and a pericardial knock early in diastole; imaging may show pericardial thickening.

diagnoses.name: Tricuspid regurgitation
diagnoses.description: Backflow into right atrium causing raised JVP with giant v wave (cv wave), edema/ascites/hepatomegaly with systolic pulsations; blowing pansystolic murmur at lower-left sternal border increased during inspiration (De Carvallo’s sign).

precomputedExplanations.description: Chronic stable angina pectoris is predictable **exertional chest discomfort** caused by transient myocardial ischemia, usually from fixed **coronary artery disease**. Symptoms are typically relieved by rest or nitrates and are not primarily driven by valvular outflow obstruction.
keySymptoms: **Exertional chest tightness/pressure** - Substernal heaviness triggered by activity, improves with rest, reflects demand–supply mismatch.
**Radiation to arm/neck/jaw** - Pain may spread along typical dermatomes due to shared spinal afferent pathways.
**Shortness of breath on exertion** - Anginal equivalent from ischemia-induced LV diastolic dysfunction and elevated filling pressures.
**Diaphoresis/nausea** - Autonomic activation accompanying ischemic discomfort, more common with more intense episodes.
**Predictable threshold pattern** - Similar exertion level reproducibly provokes symptoms over weeks to months without progression.
precomputedExplanations.clinicalReasoning: This patient’s chest discomfort is exertional, which can resemble chronic stable angina. However, the bedside cardiovascular findings strongly indicate **severe aortic stenosis**: **parvus et tardus** pulse with **apicocarotid delay**, low systolic/pulse pressure, **heaving LV apex** with palpable **S4**, **carotid shudder**, and a harsh **crescendo–decrescendo ejection systolic murmur** at the **aortic area** radiating to the neck with **late peaking**. Exertional near-syncope is a classic symptom complex of symptomatic severe **aortic stenosis** (angina–syncope–dyspnea triad). Therefore, the symptom mechanism is more consistent with fixed LV outflow obstruction than primary coronary ischemia.
precomputedExplanations.whyIncorrectForCase: Chronic stable angina does not explain the hallmark physical signs of **aortic stenosis** (e.g., **parvus et tardus**, **carotid thrill/shudder**, late-peaking **ejection systolic murmur** radiating to carotids). Exertional near-syncope in this setting is better explained by fixed outflow obstruction and inability to augment cardiac output than by uncomplicated stable angina.
keyDifferencesFromCorrect: **Murmur site and radiation** - Stable angina has no characteristic murmur; **aortic stenosis** has an **ejection systolic murmur** at aortic area radiating to carotids.
**Murmur shape and timing vs A2** - Angina: none; **aortic stenosis**: **crescendo–decrescendo** murmur that typically stops before **A2** and may be late-peaking when severe.
**Carotid pulse** - Angina: usually normal upstroke unless other disease; **aortic stenosis**: **slow-rising, low-volume (parvus et tardus)** pulse with **apicocarotid delay**.
**Syncope mechanism** - Angina: syncope is not typical and suggests arrhythmia/other cause; **aortic stenosis**: exertional syncope from fixed obstruction and reduced cerebral perfusion.
**Post-VPC intensity** - Angina: no murmur change; **aortic stenosis**: murmur intensity **increases after VPC** (post-extrasystolic potentiation).
**Apex findings** - Angina: may have normal apex; **aortic stenosis**: **heaving/thrusting LV apex** and palpable **S4** from concentric LV hypertrophy.

**No clear relief with rest/nitrates provided** - Stable angina classically improves promptly with rest or nitroglycerin; not established here.
**No evidence of normal carotid upstroke** - Stable angina should not produce **parvus et tardus**; its presence argues against angina as primary diagnosis.
**No absence of valvular signs** - Stable angina would not cause **carotid shudder**, **heaving apex**, or late-peaking **ejection murmur**; these are present.

precomputedExplanations.description: **Aortic stenosis** is obstruction to left ventricular outflow due to narrowing of the aortic valve. It causes a fixed stroke volume with pressure overload, leading to concentric LV hypertrophy, reduced systolic/pulse pressure, and exertional symptoms from inability to augment cardiac output.
keySymptoms: **Exertional chest tightness/heaviness (angina)** - Fixed outflow limits coronary perfusion reserve; LV hypertrophy increases oxygen demand during exertion.
**Exertional near-syncope/syncope** - Fixed cardiac output cannot rise with exercise, causing cerebral hypoperfusion and presyncope/fainting.
**Exertional dyspnea** - Elevated LV diastolic pressure from hypertrophy causes pulmonary venous congestion during activity.
**Parvus et tardus carotid pulse** - Slow-rising, low-volume upstroke reflects delayed ejection across a severely narrowed aortic valve.
**Apicocarotid delay** - Delay between LV impulse and carotid upstroke indicates prolonged LV ejection time in severe stenosis.
**Narrow pulse pressure / low systolic pressure** - Reduced forward stroke volume produces systolic decapitation and diminished pulse pressure.
**Heaving (thrusting) LV apex beat** - Pressure overload from stenosis causes concentric LV hypertrophy producing a sustained, forceful apex.
**Palpable LV S4** - A stiff hypertrophied LV generates a presystolic gallop from atrial contraction into noncompliant ventricle.
**Carotid shudder (thrill)** - Turbulent high-velocity systolic flow across stenotic valve transmits vibration to carotid arteries.
**Ejection systolic murmur at aortic area radiating to neck** - Harsh crescendo–decrescendo murmur with carotid radiation is classic for aortic stenosis.
**Late-peaking systolic murmur** - Later peak in systole correlates with more severe obstruction and prolonged ejection time.
**Soft/single A2 or paradoxical splitting** - Reduced aortic valve excursion delays/softens A2; severe AS can cause paradoxical splitting.
precomputedExplanations.clinicalReasoning: The symptom triad pattern of **exertional angina**, **exertional syncope/near-syncope**, and **exertional dyspnea** strongly supports symptomatic severe **aortic stenosis** due to fixed cardiac output and LV hypertrophy. Auscultation reveals a harsh **crescendo–decrescendo ejection systolic murmur** maximal at the **aortic area** with **carotid radiation** and **late peaking**, which is characteristic of severe AS. These findings also distinguish it from **mitral regurgitation**, which typically has a **pan-systolic** apical murmur continuing to **A2** and a brisk, high-volume carotid pulse.

precomputedExplanations.description: **Constrictive pericarditis** is a chronic inflammatory condition where a thickened, fibrotic (often calcified) pericardium restricts diastolic filling of the heart. This produces predominant **right-sided heart failure** physiology with elevated systemic venous pressures and reduced cardiac output, especially during exertion.
keySymptoms: **Progressive dyspnea** - Exertional breathlessness from impaired ventricular filling and reduced stroke volume.
**Fatigue/exercise intolerance** - Low cardiac output limits exertional capacity and causes early tiredness.
**Peripheral edema** - Leg swelling due to chronically elevated systemic venous pressure.
**Abdominal distension/ascites** - Hepatic congestion and fluid accumulation from right-sided venous hypertension.
**Orthopnea/PND (less prominent)** - Can occur, but systemic congestion often dominates over pulmonary edema.
**Chest discomfort (atypical)** - Usually non-anginal; may relate to inflammation rather than fixed outflow obstruction.
precomputedExplanations.clinicalReasoning: This patient’s symptom triad is classic for symptomatic **severe aortic stenosis**: exertional **angina-like chest tightness**, exertional **near-syncope**, and exertional **dyspnea**. The examination strongly supports **fixed LV outflow obstruction**: **parvus et tardus** pulse with **apicocarotid delay**, low systolic/pulse pressure, **heaving LV apex** with **S4**, and a harsh **crescendo–decrescendo ejection systolic murmur** at the **aortic area** radiating to the carotids with late peaking. Constrictive pericarditis instead produces signs of **systemic venous congestion** and characteristic diastolic findings rather than a carotid-radiating ejection murmur and slow-rising pulse.
precomputedExplanations.whyIncorrectForCase: The case lacks hallmark features of **constrictive pericarditis** such as **raised JVP**, **Kussmaul sign**, **peripheral edema/ascites**, and a **pericardial knock**. Instead, the presence of **parvus et tardus**, **carotid thrill**, and a late-peaking **ejection systolic murmur** radiating to the neck is far more consistent with **aortic stenosis**.
keyDifferencesFromCorrect: **Murmur timing/quality** - Constrictive pericarditis typically has a **pericardial knock (early diastolic)**, not a harsh **ejection systolic** murmur of **aortic stenosis**.
**Pulse character** - Constrictive pericarditis does not cause **parvus et tardus**; **aortic stenosis** causes slow-rising, low-volume carotid upstroke with **apicocarotid delay**.

**Dominant physiology** - Constrictive pericarditis causes **impaired diastolic filling** with **right-sided congestion**; **aortic stenosis** causes **fixed LV outflow obstruction** and pressure overload.

**Key bedside signs** - Constrictive pericarditis features **elevated JVP**, **Kussmaul sign**, and often **hepatomegaly/ascites**; **aortic stenosis** features **carotid shudder**, **heaving apex**, and **S4**.
**Blood pressure pattern** - Constrictive pericarditis may show normal pulse pressure; **aortic stenosis** often shows **low systolic and narrow pulse pressure (systolic decapitation)**.
missingFindings: **Raised JVP** - Expected due to systemic venous hypertension; not described in this patient.
**Kussmaul sign** - Inspiratory rise in JVP is characteristic; absence argues against constriction.
**Peripheral edema/ascites** - Common in constrictive pericarditis from right-sided failure; not present here.
**Pericardial knock** - Early diastolic sound typical of constriction; instead there is **S4** and an ejection murmur.
**Hepatomegaly/congestive hepatopathy** - Frequent with chronic constriction; not reported.
**Pulsus paradoxus (sometimes)** - May be present in pericardial disease; the case instead highlights **parvus et tardus**.

precomputedExplanations.description: **Tricuspid regurgitation (TR)** is systolic backflow of blood from the right ventricle into the right atrium due to tricuspid valve incompetence. It most often results from **right ventricular dilation** (functional TR) secondary to **pulmonary hypertension** or left-sided heart disease, producing systemic venous congestion.
keySymptoms: **Fatigue** - Reduced forward cardiac output and venous congestion cause low energy and exercise intolerance.
**Peripheral edema** - Elevated systemic venous pressure leads to ankle swelling that worsens through the day.
**Abdominal distension/ascites** - Chronic venous congestion causes fluid accumulation in the peritoneal cavity.
**Right upper quadrant discomfort** - Congestive hepatomegaly stretches liver capsule causing dull aching pain.
**Pulsations in the neck** - Prominent systolic venous waves may be noticed due to regurgitant flow.
precomputedExplanations.clinicalReasoning: This patient’s dominant syndrome is **exertional angina-like chest tightness**, **exertional near-syncope**, and **exertional dyspnea**, which is classic for symptomatic **severe aortic stenosis**. The exam strongly supports left-sided outflow obstruction: **parvus et tardus** pulse with **apicocarotid delay**, low systolic/pulse pressure, a **heaving LV apex** with **S4**, and a harsh **crescendo–decrescendo ejection systolic murmur** at the **aortic area** radiating to the **carotids** with late peaking. TR instead produces a **holosystolic murmur** best at the **left lower sternal border** that increases with inspiration and is accompanied by **right-sided congestion** findings. Therefore, TR does not explain the key symptom pattern or the hallmark arterial pulse and murmur characteristics present here.
precomputedExplanations.whyIncorrectForCase: TR typically causes **systemic venous congestion** (edema, hepatomegaly, ascites, raised JVP) rather than exertional **angina/syncope** from fixed LV outflow obstruction. The patient’s murmur is an **ejection systolic** murmur at the **base** radiating to the **carotids** with **parvus et tardus**, which is inconsistent with TR.
keyDifferencesFromCorrect: **Murmur timing/shape** - TR is **pan/holosystolic**; **aortic stenosis** is **ejection (crescendo–decrescendo)** and ends before **A2**.
**Murmur location** - TR is loudest at **left lower sternal border**; **aortic stenosis** is loudest at **aortic area** and may be heard at apex.
**Radiation** - TR radiates to **right sternal border/epigastrium**; **aortic stenosis** radiates to **carotids/neck**.
**Respiratory variation** - TR increases with **inspiration (Carvallo sign)**; **aortic stenosis** typically does not show this pattern.
**Pulse character** - TR does not cause **parvus et tardus**; **aortic stenosis** causes **slow-rising, low-volume** carotid pulse with **apicocarotid delay**.
**Hemodynamic syndrome** - TR causes **right-sided failure** signs; **aortic stenosis** causes **fixed LV outflow obstruction** with exertional **syncope/angina/dyspnea**.
missingFindings: **Raised JVP with prominent v waves** - Typical of TR; not described, arguing against significant right-sided regurgitation.
**Pansystolic murmur at left lower sternal border** - Expected in TR; instead murmur is **ejection systolic** at the **aortic area**.
**Carvallo sign (inspiratory augmentation)** - Classic for TR; no inspiratory increase is reported.
**Pulsatile hepatomegaly** - Suggests severe TR with systolic hepatic pulsations; not present in the case.
**Peripheral edema/ascites** - Common TR congestion features; absent from the presentation.
**Right ventricular heave** - Supports RV volume overload from TR; exam instead shows **heaving LV apex** and **S4**.

keyHistoryQuestions.action: Ask about exertional breathlessness and reduced exercise tolerance (including orthopnea/PND).
keyHistoryQuestions.reasoning: Dyspnea/exercise intolerance is part of the symptomatic triad and reflects cardiac decompensation/heart failure in aortic stenosis; symptoms are a good index of severity.
keyHistoryQuestions.expectedFinding: Exertional dyspnea and/or orthopnea/PND suggesting heart failure symptoms in AS.
keyHistoryQuestions.textbookReference: “Symptomatic triad of aortic stenosis… (1) breathlessness (dyspnea)… Heart failure: Orthopnea and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea (PND).”

keyHistoryQuestions.reasoning: Angina is a cardinal symptom of AS due to mismatch in myocardial oxygen demand–supply ratio or coexistent CAD.
keyHistoryQuestions.expectedFinding: Typical exertional angina in a patient suspected of AS.
keyHistoryQuestions.textbookReference: “Angina is typical exertional and is due to mismatch in myocardial oxygen demand-supply ratio, or coexistent coronary artery disease (CAD).”

keyHistoryQuestions.action: Ask about exertional syncope or presyncope (near-fainting) and its triggers (walking/exertion).
keyHistoryQuestions.reasoning: Exertional syncope is a cardinal symptom of AS due to failure of cardiac output to rise with exertion leading to fall in BP.
keyHistoryQuestions.expectedFinding: Exertional syncope/presyncope episodes consistent with fixed outflow obstruction.
keyHistoryQuestions.textbookReference: “Exertional syncope (or presyncope): Due to failure of cardiac output to rise to meet demand, leading to a fall in BP.”

keyHistoryQuestions.action: Ask whether the patient has been asymptomatic until a murmur was found incidentally during routine examination, and clarify duration/progression of symptoms over months.
keyHistoryQuestions.reasoning: AS is commonly diagnosed in asymptomatic patients during routine clinical examination; symptom onset helps judge severity and prognosis.
keyHistoryQuestions.expectedFinding: History of incidental murmur earlier and gradual development of exertional symptoms (months).
keyHistoryQuestions.textbookReference: “It is commonly diagnosed in asymptomatic patients during routine clinical examination.”

keyExaminations.action: Auscultate for an ejection mid-systolic (crescendo–decrescendo/diamond-shaped) murmur best heard in the aortic area, radiating to the neck (carotids), and assess relation to A2 (stops before A2).
keyExaminations.reasoning: The characteristic murmur pattern and radiation are key bedside identifiers of AS; relation to A2 helps differentiate from pansystolic MR.
keyExaminations.expectedFinding: Harsh/rough ejection mid-systolic murmur at aortic area radiating to carotids; stops before A2; late peaking suggests severe AS.
keyExaminations.textbookReference: “Ejection mid-systolic murmur… radiates to the neck (to carotids arteries)… Best heard in the base of heart (aortic area)… diamond-shaped (crescendo decrescendo)… with late peaking in severe AS.”

keyExaminations.action: Palpate carotid pulse for slow-rising, low-volume pulse (parvus et tardus) and check for carotid shudder; assess for apico-carotid delay.
keyExaminations.reasoning: Pulse contour (slow rising, low volume) and apico-carotid delay are classic signs; apico-carotid delay indicates severe AS.
keyExaminations.expectedFinding: Parvus and tardus pulse; carotid shudder; apico-carotid delay (severe AS).
keyExaminations.textbookReference: “Parvus and tardus pulse: Slow rising, late peaking, and low amplitude… Carotid shudder… Apico-carotid delay is seen in severe aortic stenosis.”

keyExaminations.action: Assess apex beat character and presence of S4 (palpable/auscultatory).
keyExaminations.reasoning: AS causes LV pressure overload leading to heaving/thrusting apex; severe AS is associated with S4.
keyExaminations.expectedFinding: Thrusting/heaving LV type apex beat; S4 (especially in severe AS).
keyExaminations.textbookReference: “Apex beat: Thrusting/heaving LV type apex beat due to LV pressure overload… Palpable LV S4… Severe… S4.”

keyExaminations.action: Assess second heart sound (A2) for softness/single S2 and look for paradoxical split S2 in suspected severe AS.
keyExaminations.reasoning: A2 changes and paradoxical split S2 are severity markers in AS.
keyExaminations.expectedFinding: Soft A2; paradoxical (reversed) split S2 in severe AS.
keyExaminations.textbookReference: “S2-A2: Soft… In severe AS, paradoxical (reversed) split of second heart sound A2.”

keyInvestigations.reasoning: ECG can show LV hypertrophy and rhythm/conduction abnormalities described in AS (AF; AV conduction defects/IVCD in calcific AS).
keyInvestigations.expectedFinding: Left ventricular hypertrophy; possible atrial fibrillation (10–15%); possible AV conduction defects/IVCD (5% of calcific AS).
keyInvestigations.textbookReference: “ECG: Left ventricular hypertrophy… Atrial fibrillation in 10–15%… AV conduction defects and IVCD in 5% of calcific AS.”

keyInvestigations.reasoning: Chest X-ray may show concentric LVH effects (rounding of apex with normal/small heart), post-stenotic dilatation of ascending aorta, and valve calcification.
keyInvestigations.expectedFinding: Rounding of apex due to concentric LVH with normal/small heart; prominent dilation of ascending aorta; possible aortic valve calcification.
keyInvestigations.textbookReference: “Chest X-ray: Rounding of apex due to concentric left ventricular hypertrophy… Prominent dilation of ascending aorta… Calcification of aortic valve (if present).”

keyInvestigations.action: Order transthoracic echocardiography to evaluate severity and gradient across the aortic valve.
keyInvestigations.reasoning: Echo is the key noninvasive test to evaluate severity and gradient in AS.
keyInvestigations.expectedFinding: Quantification of severity and gradient across the aortic valve consistent with AS.
keyInvestigations.textbookReference: “Echocardiography: Helps in evaluation of severity and gradient across the aortic valve.”

keyInvestigations.action: Order Doppler (echocardiographic Doppler) to detect severity of stenosis and associated aortic regurgitation.
keyInvestigations.reasoning: Doppler is specifically noted as useful for detecting severity and identifying associated AR.
keyInvestigations.expectedFinding: Doppler evidence of stenosis severity; detection of associated aortic regurgitation if present.
keyInvestigations.textbookReference: “Doppler: Useful for detecting the severity of stenosis and associated aortic regurgitation.”

keyInvestigations.action: If needed, order cardiac CT/cardiac MR to assess thoracic aorta for aneurysm, dissection, or coarctation.
keyInvestigations.reasoning: Advanced imaging may be required to assess associated thoracic aortic pathology.
keyInvestigations.expectedFinding: Assessment for presence/absence of aneurysm, dissection, or coarctation of thoracic aorta.
keyInvestigations.textbookReference: “Cardiac magnetic resonance and cardiac CT: They may be required for assessing the presence of aneurysm, dissection, or coarctation of thoracic aorta.”

differentialDiagnoses.name: Mitral regurgitation
differentialDiagnoses.howToRuleOut: Use murmur characteristics and pulse findings: MR is pansystolic at apex and continues till A2; post-VPC intensity shows no change/decreases; carotid pulse is quick rising high volume. AS is ejection mid-systolic, stops before A2, post-VPC intensity increases, and carotid pulse is slow rising low volume.
differentialDiagnoses.textbookReference: “Aortic stenosis… ejection-mid systolic. Stops before A2… Post-VPC intensity increases… Carotid pulse slow rising, low volume… Mitral regurgitation… Pan systolic. Continues till A2… No change/decreases… Quick rising high volume.”

differentialDiagnoses.name: Aortic regurgitation with associated systolic murmur (e.g., functional systolic murmur across aortic valve)
differentialDiagnoses.howToRuleOut: Look for AR peripheral signs and pulse pressure features: AR has bounding/collapsing pulses and wide pulse pressure; AS typically has low systolic and pulse pressures with parvus et tardus (unless coexistent AR/HTN). Also Doppler helps detect associated AR.
differentialDiagnoses.textbookReference: “Peripheral pulses… bounding, or collapsing… increased/wide pulse pressure… In AS… Low systolic and pulse pressures… Parvus and tardus pulse… Doppler… associated aortic regurgitation.”

differentialDiagnoses.name: Pulmonary stenosis (as another cause of ejection systolic murmur)
differentialDiagnoses.howToRuleOut: Recognize that pulmonary stenosis is listed among causes of mid-systolic/ejection systolic murmurs; differentiate by localizing murmur to aortic area with carotid radiation and AS pulse findings (parvus et tardus).
differentialDiagnoses.textbookReference: “Mid-systolic/ejection systolic murmurs: Aortic stenosis… Pulmonary stenosis…”

idealPathway.diagnosticApproach: 1) Elicit textbook symptom triad and heart failure symptoms: exertional dyspnea/exercise intolerance (± orthopnea/PND), exertional angina, and exertional syncope/presyncope. 2) Perform focused cardiovascular exam: identify ejection mid-systolic (crescendo–decrescendo) murmur at aortic area radiating to carotids and stopping before A2; assess severity markers (late peaking murmur, soft A2/paradoxical split S2, S4, apico-carotid delay, anacrotic/parvus et tardus pulse). 3) Order investigations in cost-effective sequence: ECG (LVH/AF/conduction defects), chest X-ray (concentric LVH effects, post-stenotic ascending aorta dilatation, valve calcification), then echocardiography to evaluate severity and gradient; add Doppler to grade stenosis and detect associated AR. 4) If needed, use cardiac CT/CMR to assess thoracic aorta (aneurysm/dissection/coarctation). 5) Differentiate from similar conditions using Table 1.74 (especially MR) and pulse/BP features (AS low-volume slow-rising pulse vs AR bounding/wide pulse pressure).
